name: Germany (Weimar Republic and Nazi Germany)
summary: Germany between the fall of the Kaiser (1918) and defeat in the Second World War (1945): the democratic Weimar Republic, then from 1933 Hitler’s Nazi dictatorship, which started the war in Europe and carried out the Holocaust.

terrain.value: North European Plain, central uplands, Alps.

climate.value: Temperate, with cold winters and mild summers.

resources.value: Coal in the Ruhr, iron, potash and farmland.

disasters.value: The Great Depression from 1929, worsened by the 1931 European banking crisis, hit Germany severely.

urbanisation.value: Berlin, Hamburg, Munich and the Ruhr cities were the largest.

disease.value: The 1918 influenza pandemic killed many, and food shortages after the First World War also harmed health.

migration.value: Jews and opponents fled after 1933; millions forced labourers brought in during the war.

economicBase.value: Heavy industry, chemicals, engineering and a large armaments sector under the Nazis.

tradeRoutes.value: Railways, the Rhine and the port of Hamburg carried goods.

wealth.value: Reparations, hyperinflation peaking in 1923, and a surge in unemployment after 1929.

moneyAndTax.value: Paper mark, then the Rentenmark (November 1923), which stopped the hyperinflation.

inequality.value: Unemployment hit workers hardest; Jews were robbed of property after 1933.

governmentType.value: Parliamentary republic (1919–33), then a one-party dictatorship.

keyRulers.value: Friedrich Ebert. Gustav Stresemann. Paul von Hindenburg. Adolf Hitler.

succession.value: Elections; Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor (January 1933), and on Hindenburg’s death (1934) Hitler became “Führer and Reich Chancellor”.

institutions.value: Weimar Constitution (1919); Enabling Act (1933) ended democracy.

stability.value: Two attempted coups (Kapp Putsch 1920, beer hall putsch 1923), political murders and street fighting.

eliteConflict.value: Army leaders gained growing political influence; President Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor in 1933.

armyAndTech.value: Versailles limited the army (Reichswehr) to 100,000 men, which it secretly tried to get around.

majorWars.value: The Second World War (1939–45), which Germany started by invading Poland.

territoryChange.value: Treaty of Versailles (1919): lost its colonies and about 13% of its European territory.

alliancesRivals.value: The Axis alliance with Italy and Japan, and war against Britain, France, the Soviet Union and the United States.

inventions.value: Jet aircraft (the Me 262) and the V-2 rocket were developed, and the Autobahn network was expanded.

scienceEducation.value: World-leading science until scientists were expelled from 1933.

openness.value: Open in the 1920s; closed and autarkic under the Nazis.

communicationTransport.value: Radio was used for propaganda; railways carried both goods and deported people, and the Autobahn was built.

artsArchitecture.value: Weimar culture: Bauhaus architecture, cinema, cabaret and jazz.

sharedIdentity.value: Widespread anger at the Versailles Treaty’s war-guilt clause (Article 231) and territorial losses.

dailyLife.value: Apartments in cities, with rationing and bombing during the war.

neighbours.value: France, Poland, Austria, Czechoslovakia, Netherlands, Denmark.

ideasReligions.value: Nazism; antisemitism; the Holocaust killed about six million Jews.

colonisation.value: Lost its colonies under the Treaty of Versailles (1919).

declineSignals.value: The Depression, then Hitler’s one-party dictatorship (1933).

outcome.value: Defeated in 1945; divided into occupation zones, later West and East Germany.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
